description.summary: A spider trickster of Akan oral tradition, originating among the Ashanti people of present-day Ghana and carried by enslaved West Africans across the Atlantic, where Anansi became one of the central figures of Caribbean and African-American folklore.
description.full: Anansi (Akan: Ananse) is a spider trickster figure of Akan oral tradition, especially associated with the Ashanti people of present-day Ghana. The name itself means 'spider' in Akan, and Anansi is variously depicted as a literal spider, an anthropomorphic spider with a human face, or a human-shaped figure with spider-like features. Anansi is the central character of a vast cycle of folktales known in Akan as Anansesem ('Spider Stories'). Two foundational Anansi tales are widely retold: in one, Anansi acquires all stories from the sky-god Nyame by completing a series of impossible tasks, becoming the owner of all stories; in another, Anansi tries to hoard all wisdom in a clay pot, only to break it and disperse wisdom across the world. The Atlantic slave trade carried Anansi narratives to the Caribbean and the Americas, where he survived under names such as Anancy (Jamaica), Aunt Nancy (American South), Kompa Nanzi (Curaçao), and Bro Nansi. In the diaspora, Anansi tales served as resistance narratives that valorised the cleverness of the apparently weak. Anansi has been the subject of substantial 20th- and 21st-century literary adaptation, including Neil Gaiman's 'American Gods' (2001) and 'Anansi Boys' (2005), and remains a living oral tradition in West Africa and the Caribbean.

etymology.meaning: 'Spider'; in narrative usage, the trickster spider figure.
etymology.first_use: Long-standing in Akan oral tradition; recorded in colonial-era ethnography from the late 19th century onward.

related_phenomena.name: Br'er Rabbit
related_phenomena.description: African-American trickster figure with overlapping motifs

features.description: A literal spider, sometimes with eight legs and human face

physical.morphology: Variable across tellings: literal spider, anthropomorphic spider, or human with spider features.

abilities.description: Anansi defeats stronger opponents through speech, persuasion, and trickery
Anansi shifts between spider and human forms across tales
After winning the sky-god's stories, Anansi is the owner of all tales

range.description: Originating among the Akan peoples of present-day Ghana and carried through the Atlantic slave trade across West Africa, the Caribbean, and the Americas.

peak_activity_periods.description: Atlantic slave trade carries Anansi traditions to the Caribbean and Americas
Major scholarly documentation by R. S. Rattray and Peggy Appiah

origins.cultural_roots: Akan oral tradition, especially among the Ashanti of central Ghana.
origins.earliest_accounts: Long pre-colonial Akan oral tradition; documented in writing from late-19th-century ethnography onward.
origins.folklore_connections: Anansesem are part of a vast Akan and broader West African storytelling tradition; the figure resonates with other trickster archetypes worldwide.

timeline.event: R. S. Rattray publishes 'Akan-Ashanti Folk-Tales', collecting Anansi tales in Twi and English
timeline.significance: Foundational ethnographic record of the Anansi corpus
timeline.source: Rattray, R. S. (1930), Akan-Ashanti Folk-Tales, Oxford University Press

timeline.event: Peggy Appiah publishes 'Ananse the Spider: Tales from an Ashanti Village'
timeline.significance: Influential English-language retelling for general readers

timeline.event: Neil Gaiman publishes the novel 'Anansi Boys'
timeline.significance: Major 21st-century literary engagement with the Anansi tradition

history.modern_era: Anansi remains a living tradition in Ghana and across the Caribbean, taught in schools, performed in oral traditions, and adapted in literature, comics, television, and games.

documentary.name: Akan-Ashanti Folk-Tales (Rattray)
documentary.description: R. S. Rattray's bilingual collection of Akan-Ashanti folk tales, including a substantial body of Anansesem.

paranormal.name: Trickster deity
paranormal.description: In Akan tradition, Anansi has the standing of a trickster deity and culture-hero, mediating between the sky-god Nyame and humanity.
evidence_cited: Continuity of Anansi narrative across the diaspora

skeptical.name: Cultural-archetypal trickster
skeptical.description: Folklorists analyse Anansi as one of the world's most fully developed examples of the trickster archetype, performing social and pedagogical work in narrative.

stories: How Anansi Got the Stories from Nyame

Anansi and the Tar Baby (cognate of Br'er Rabbit)
folklore.beliefs: Anansi tales serve as moral, comic, and educational instruction; in the diaspora, they additionally function as narratives of resistance and survival.

indigenous.significance: Anansi is a central figure in Akan culture and a touchstone of African-diasporic identity.
indigenous.sensitivity_note: Anansi tales are a living tradition; they should be presented with attribution to Akan and diasporic source communities.
indigenous.respect_guidelines: Cite Akan tellers, Caribbean storytellers, and recognised folklorists; avoid divorcing Anansi from his cultural and historical context.
